The Riemann Hypothesis. All non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie on a single vertical line in the complex plane. Proposed by Bernhard Riemann in his seminal 1859 paper, the hypothesis provides deep insight into the distribution of prime numbers. If true, it would establish the tightest possible bounds on the error term of the Prime Number Theorem and confirm that prime numbers are distributed as regularly as possible. Due to its foundational status and difficulty, it has been designated as one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, carrying a one-million-dollar reward for its resolution. The Riemann Zeta Function is defined as the infinite sum from n equals one to infinity of n to the power of negative s, defined for complex numbers with real part greater than one. It can be analytically continued to the entire complex plane except for a simple pole at s equals one. The function has trivial zeros at all negative even integers: s equals negative two, negative four, negative six, and so on. The non-trivial zeros lie within the critical strip, where the real part of s is between zero and one. The Riemann Hypothesis asserts that all these non-trivial zeros actually lie on the critical line where the real part of s equals one-half. Riemann showed that the distribution of primes is intimately linked to the locations of the non-trivial zeros. The proof of the Prime Number Theorem relies on showing that no zeros lie on the boundary lines where the real part of s equals one and where it equals zero. If the hypothesis is true, the number of primes up to x, denoted π of x, is approximated by the logarithmic integral of x with an error term bounded by the square root of x times the logarithm of x. This is the optimal possible bound. The hypothesis is equivalent to statements about the growth of the Möbius function. Specifically, the bound on M of x of O of x to the power of one-half plus epsilon is equivalent to the Riemann Hypothesis. The hypothesis is also equivalent to Robin's theorem, a statement about the divisor function. Computational searches have verified that the first ten trillion non-trivial zeros lie precisely on the critical line, but this does not constitute a mathematical proof. The Hilbert-Pólya Conjecture suggests that the zeros of the zeta function correspond to the eigenvalues of a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space. This has connected the Riemann Hypothesis to quantum mechanics and random matrix theory, opening doors to physical approaches to the problem. The Clay Mathematics Institute named the Riemann Hypothesis one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems in two thousand, offering a one million dollar reward for its proof or disproof. The Riemann Hypothesis is widely regarded as the holy grail of modern pure mathematics. Hundreds of mathematical theorems begin with the clause "Assuming the Riemann Hypothesis is true." Its formulation in 1859 marked the birth of analytic number theory, transforming the study of discrete prime numbers through the continuous tools of complex analysis. In mathematics education and competitions, the hypothesis and the zeta function are frequent subjects. Clues focus on the definition of the critical line, trivial versus non-trivial zeros, its equivalent formulation via Robin's inequality, or the Hilbert-Pólya conjecture linking it to physical spectral operators. The hypothesis also provides the optimal error bound for the prime density function described by the Prime Number Theorem. The Euler product formula for the zeta function connects it directly to all primes. Dirichlet L-functions, which generalize the Riemann zeta function, arise in Dirichlet's Theorem on Arithmetic Progressions. Other famous unsolved prime conjectures like Goldbach's conjecture are related through analytic methods. Prime gaps are bounded and studied using tools from the zeta function in connection with the Twin Prime Conjecture.
